Write a covariance matrix as the cells a ctsem model reads

Source: R/ctCov.R
ctCov.Rd

ctsem's covariance matrices (T0VAR, DIFFUSION, MANIFESTVAR, and the population spreads RAWPOPVAR and RAWPOPVAR_<idname>) are specified as a lower triangle, with standard deviations on the diagonal and, below it, values that the model's covmattransform turns into correlations. Except for two variables under 'z', where each value is Fisher's z of the correlation, the correlations depend on all the values together, so the cells for a given covariance are hard to work out by hand. ctCov() computes them.

Usage

ctCov(cov, covmattransform = "z")

Arguments

cov

A symmetric positive definite covariance matrix.

covmattransform

The construction to write the cells for: 'z' (the default, and what ctModel uses), 'rawcorr' or 'cholesky'. A ctCov() matrix assigned into a model is rewritten for that model's own construction, so this matters only when the cells are read directly.

Value

The cells, a lower triangular numeric matrix of class ctCov, with the covariance as attribute covariance. 'rawcorr' cannot reach every correlation matrix, and a covariance it cannot represent is refused.

Details

Use the result wherever a fixed matrix can go, such as ctModel(DIFFUSION = ctCov(S)), m$matrices$T0VAR <- ctCov(S), or m$RAWPOPVAR <- ctCov(S), always for the whole matrix. The model also stores the covariance, so the matrix keeps its meaning if covmattransform is changed later, and the R generator of ctGenerate, which reads covariance cells as a Cholesky factor, generates from the same covariance as the julia generator. A cell edited by hand afterwards replaces what ctCov() wrote.

For RAWPOPVAR, the covariance is that of the raw, untransformed parameters across subjects (or groups, for RAWPOPVAR_<idname>), which is the scale a fit reports it on.

Examples

S <- matrix(c(1, .6, .3,
              .6, 2, .5,
              .3, .5, 1.5), 3)
ctCov(S)

m <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(3), DIFFUSION = ctCov(S), Tpoints = 5)
